A production network becomes singular due to substitution elasticity when the elasticity of substitution (σ) is nonneutral (either inelastic σ < 1 or elastic σ > 1), causing the network to transform in a way that creates extreme conditions. Specifically:

- For inelastic networks (σ < 1), the network can reach "negative singularity" where an immense amount of labor becomes necessary to offset other production factors (m0 → ∞).
- For elastic networks (σ > 1), the network can reach "positive singularity" where only minimal labor is needed to offset other factors (m0 → 0).

These singularities arise because nonneutral substitution elasticity makes the economy-wide production network unstable against sectoral productivity shocks, leading to nonlinear network transformations that can make certain commodities impossible to produce (negative singularity) or require minimal input (positive singularity). This phenomenon stems from the unlimited factor substitution possibilities in the CES production function's isoquant.
